title: Count Ships on a Radar Grid
statement:
A radar screen is a grid of cells. "X" is part of a ship and "." is open water.

Every ship is a straight line of "X" cells, one cell wide: either a horizontal run in one row or a vertical run in one column. No two ships share an edge, so they are always separated by water up, down, left and right. Corners may touch.

Return the number of ships on the screen.

examples.why: A vertical ship of length 3 on the left, a one-cell ship in the top right, and a horizontal ship of length 2 in the bottom right.
The two cells only touch at a corner, so they are two separate ships. Treating diagonals as connected would give 1.

constraints: The grid is a valid placement as described
hints: Ships are groups of X cells connected through shared edges. Counting connected groups is a flood fill.
Because every ship is a straight line and ships never share an edge, each ship has exactly one top-left cell. What is special about that cell's neighbours?
Count the X cells that have no X directly above them and no X directly to their left. One pass, no extra memory, no changes to the grid.

explain.intuition:
The general tool is a flood fill: every time you find an unvisited X, count one ship and mark its whole connected group as visited. That works for any shapes.

The rules here allow a shortcut. Each ship is a straight line, and ships never share an edge. So every ship has exactly one head: its top cell if vertical, its left cell if horizontal. The head is the only cell of the ship with no X above it and no X to its left. Any other ship cell has its predecessor right there. So counting heads counts ships, in one read-only pass.
steps: Visit every cell (r, c) in row order.
Skip it if the cell above (r − 1) or to the left (c − 1) is also "X": it continues a ship already counted.
Otherwise it is a head: increment count.
pitfalls: Counting all X cells. A ship of length 3 is one ship, not three.
Treating diagonal neighbours as the same ship. Corners may touch, as in the second example.
Reading grid[r − 1] or grid[r][c − 1] without bounds checks on the first row or column.

solutions.title: Flood fill each ship
solutions.idea: Scan the grid. At each unvisited X, count a ship and mark every X connected to it through shared edges.

solutions.title: Count ship heads
solutions.idea: Every ship has exactly one cell with no X above it and no X to its left. Count those cells.

followups: Ships may now be any shape, like Tetris pieces. Which of the two solutions still works?
Also verify the grid is valid: every group is a straight line and no two ships share an edge.
